title: Primary Function of the System
learningObjectives: Connect cable guidance to robot motion.
student: State the function of the robot dress pack and explain why controlling cable routing is mechanically important.
instructor: The dress pack guides and protects moving power, data, and control cables. Controlling the route limits local curvature and the associated longitudinal bending strain as robot joints move.

title: Source of Mechanical Demand
learningObjectives: Recognize curvature imposed by motion without an assigned transverse load.
student: Identify what robot motion produces the local cable bend. Explain why the problem can be analyzed through imposed curvature even though no external transverse force is specified.
instructor: Relative motion of robot links and routing guides imposes a changing cable path. Curvature is a kinematic input here, so no transverse force is needed to calculate the geometric strain distribution.

title: Routing Constraint
learningObjectives: Interpret the documented radius as an inner bend radius.
student: State the documented minimum dynamic bend-radius requirement for the selected robotic cable and identify where that radius is measured.
instructor: The selected cable requires a minimum dynamic inner bend radius of 10d. For the baseline diameter this is 95 mm, measured at the inner curvature rather than at the cable centerline.

title: Mechanical Response
student: Identify the dominant response evaluated and distinguish curvature from longitudinal bending strain.
instructor: Curvature describes how rapidly the cable centerline changes direction per unit arc length. Longitudinal strain varies through the equivalent diameter according to distance from the neutral axis.

title: Critical Location
student: For a cable bent into a circular arc, identify where the magnitude of longitudinal bending strain is greatest.
instructor: The magnitude is greatest at the inner and outer cable surfaces because they are farthest from the centerline neutral axis, at y = plus or minus d/2.

title: Relevant Parameters
student: Identify the independent geometric quantities needed to evaluate curvature and maximum bending strain.
instructor: The independent inputs are equivalent cable diameter d and specified inner bend radius R_i. The centerline radius R_n and radius ratio beta are derived.

title: Model Limitation
learningObjectives: Avoid an unsupported homogeneous stress model.
student: Explain why the calculated geometric strain should not automatically be converted to cable stress using one value of E for the complete cable.
instructor: A real cable is a composite assembly with conductors, strand lay, shielding, insulation, jacket, interfaces, and slip. A single homogeneous modulus would not represent those constituent responses.

title: Student-Generated Structural Idealization
learningObjectives: Construct the local circular-arc cable model.
student: Sketch a local cable segment as a circular annulus bent into an arc. Show the inner bend radius R_i, cable diameter d, neutral-axis or centerline radius R_n, center of curvature, and the inner and outer surfaces.
instructor: A complete model shows R_i to the inner surface, d across the cable, R_n = R_i + d/2 to the cable centerline, and the inner and outer fibers at y = minus or plus d/2 under a stated convention.

title: Modeling Assumptions
student: State the assumptions used to obtain the simplified curvature-strain model.
instructor: Assume a local circular arc of constant curvature, an equivalent circular diameter, a neutral axis at the geometric centerline, and plane-section kinematics only for geometric strain. Treat the documented bend radius as the inner radius. Exclude strand slip, lay, shielding, jacket and insulation behavior, torsion, contact, fatigue, and viscoelastic effects.

title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
student: Outline the calculation sequence before substituting numbers.
instructor: Obtain d and R_i; convert to R_n; calculate curvature; apply epsilon_x = -y kappa; evaluate the magnitude at y = plus or minus d/2; derive the radius-ratio sensitivity; and make a bounded routing recommendation.

title: Convert Inner Radius to Neutral-Axis Radius
learningObjectives: Convert the manufacturer's inner radius to centerline radius.
student: Determine the cable neutral-axis or centerline radius R_n from the specified inner bend radius and cable diameter.

title: Cable Curvature
learningObjectives: Calculate curvature in two unit systems.
student: Calculate centerline curvature kappa = 1/R_n in mm-1 and m-1.

title: Longitudinal Strain Distribution
student: Using epsilon_x = -y kappa, write the longitudinal geometric strain distribution through the equivalent cable diameter and identify the neutral axis.
instructor: epsilon_x(y) = -y/R_n. The strain is zero at the cable centerline y = 0 and varies linearly to equal-and-opposite extreme values at y = plus or minus d/2.

title: Maximum Bending Strain
student: Calculate the magnitude of maximum longitudinal geometric bending strain at y = plus or minus d/2. Report the result as a decimal and percentage.

title: Radius-Ratio Form
student: Let beta = R_i/d. Derive |epsilon_max| in terms of beta and explain why cable diameter cancels when bend radius is specified as a multiple of diameter.
instructor: For beta = {{robot_cable_beta}}, {{robot_cable_beta_expression}}. Diameter cancels because both the extreme-fiber distance and centerline radius scale linearly with d.

title: Sensitivity to Routing Radius
learningObjectives: Relate larger radius ratio to lower strain.
student: For two inner bend-radius factors beta_1 and beta_2, derive epsilon_max,2/epsilon_max,1 without assigning another arbitrary radius. State what happens to strain as beta increases.
instructor: epsilon_max,2/epsilon_max,1 = (beta_1 + 1/2)/(beta_2 + 1/2). Therefore increasing beta decreases curvature and maximum geometric strain magnitude.

title: Engineering Assessment and Recommendation
learningObjectives: Assess the documented routing criterion without overstating the model.
student: Assess whether the specified route satisfies the documented minimum inner bend-radius factor of 10d. Explain why a tighter route should not be recommended using this model and state the principal limitations.
